questions.title: Design a Distributed Rate Limiter
questions.direct_answer: Use the Token Bucket algorithm backed by Redis for distributed state. Each API key gets a bucket in Redis with a Lua script for atomic check-and-decrement. Return 429 with Retry-After header when the bucket is empty. Deploy at the API gateway layer.

sections.title: Quantifying the Problem: Why This Can't Be a Database Lookup
sections.content:
**10 million requests/day ÷ 86,400 seconds ≈ 115 requests/second** average. But traffic isn't uniform — peaks run 10–50× average, so the rate limiter must handle **1,000–5,000 requests/second**. The limiter sits in the hot path of every single request, which means it must add **less than 5ms overhead**. That constraint eliminates databases (1–10ms per query with row locks under concurrency) and points to **Redis** — sub-millisecond reads/writes, atomic operations via Lua scripting, and built-in key expiration.

The deeper constraint: multiple API gateway instances sit behind a load balancer. If each instance tracks limits locally, a client can multiply their quota by the number of instances. The rate limit state must be **centralized** — all instances checking the same counter. Redis serves as that shared state store.

Rate limiting solves three problems simultaneously: **protection** (one misbehaving client can't crash the service for everyone), **fairness** (shared infrastructure across thousands of consumers), and **cost control** (cloud bills scale linearly with unbounded traffic). It's also the first defense layer against DDoS — before WAF rules even evaluate, the rate limiter can reject known-abusive keys.

sections.title: Algorithm Trade-offs: Why Token Bucket Wins for APIs
sections.content:
Four algorithms appear in rate limiter design. The decision comes down to whether you need to **allow bursts** and how much **memory per client** you can afford.

| Algorithm | How It Works | Burst Handling | Memory | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Fixed Window** | Counter per client, reset each minute | Allows 2× burst at window boundary | O(1) per client | Client sends 100 at :59, 100 at :00 = 200 in 2 sec |
| **Sliding Window Log** | Stores every request timestamp, counts within sliding window | Precise, no boundary burst | O(N) per client — expensive | 100K clients × 100 timestamps = 10M entries |
| **Sliding Window Counter** | Weighted average across current + previous window | Good approximation, low memory | O(1) per client | Approximation — not exact |
| **Token Bucket** | Bucket with capacity C (burst), refill rate R (sustained) | Two independent knobs | O(1) per client | Slightly more complex to implement |

**Token Bucket** is the industry standard — Amazon, Stripe, and Cloudflare all use it. The two-knob design separates burst behavior (capacity) from sustained throughput (refill rate). Example: capacity=10, refill=1/sec. A client can burst 10 requests instantly, then sustains 1/sec. No window boundaries, constant memory, intuitive configuration.

**Fixed Window** is tempting because it's simple, but the boundary burst problem is disqualifying for production. A client with a 100/min limit can legally send 200 requests in 2 seconds by timing requests at the window edge.

sections.title: The Atomicity Problem: Why Redis Lua Scripts Are Non-Negotiable
sections.content:
The token bucket algorithm requires three operations: read the current token count, calculate refill based on elapsed time, and decrement if tokens are available. If these execute as separate Redis commands, **two concurrent requests can both read `tokens=1` and both pass** — the same double-spending problem that plagues financial systems.

Redis `MULTI`/`EXEC` transactions don't solve this because they can't branch on intermediate results — you can't read the token count and then decide whether to decrement within a transaction. The solution is a **Lua script** executed via `EVAL`, which runs atomically on the Redis server with no interleaving possible.

The script implements lazy refill — instead of a background process ticking tokens, it calculates earned tokens based on elapsed time since the last request. This means inactive keys cost zero CPU.

```lua
local key = KEYS[1]
local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local refill_rate = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now = tonumber(ARGV[3])

local bucket = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'last_refill')
local tokens = tonumber(bucket[1]) or capacity
local last = tonumber(bucket[2]) or now

local elapsed = (now - last) / 1000
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * refill_rate)

if tokens >= 1 then
    tokens = tokens - 1
    redis.call('HMSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'last_refill', now)
    redis.call('EXPIRE', key, 3600)          -- auto-cleanup inactive keys
    return {1, math.floor(tokens)}           -- allowed, remaining
else
    return {0, 0}                            -- denied
end
```

The `EXPIRE` on every call ensures that keys for clients who stop sending requests are automatically cleaned up. Without it, Redis memory grows unboundedly as new API keys accumulate.

sections.title: Fail-Open Design: When the Rate Limiter Itself Goes Down
Multi-Tier Limits and Production Operations
sections.content:
Real systems need **multiple limit dimensions** enforced simultaneously. A single per-minute limit doesn't distinguish between a burst of 100 requests in 1 second (which might overwhelm a downstream service) and 100 requests spread across 60 seconds (which is fine).

| Tier | /sec | /min | /hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free | 5 | 20 | 500 |
| Pro | 20 | 100 | 5,000 |
| Enterprise | 100 | 1,000 | 50,000 |

Each dimension uses a separate Redis key with its own token bucket. A request is allowed only if **all buckets** have tokens. The `Retry-After` header reflects whichever limit resets soonest. Cache the API key → tier mapping locally (don't query the database per request).

**Global rate limits** protect total infrastructure capacity independent of per-key limits. If the system can handle 50,000 req/sec total, a global limiter prevents 1,000 Enterprise clients from collectively exceeding that.

**Monitoring** closes the loop: track `requests.total` (allowed/denied), `limiter.latency_p99` (must stay under 2ms), and `redis.errors`. Alert on Redis errors lasting more than 10 seconds. Dashboard the top keys by volume and by denial rate — a key consistently hitting limits either needs a higher tier or is misbehaving.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Token bucket allows controlled bursting** — the bucket refills at a fixed rate but can hold surplus tokens.
- **Sliding window log prevents boundary exploitation** — fixed window allows 2× the limit by sending 100 at 00:59 and 100 at 01:01.
- **Redis INCR + EXPIRE for distributed state** — atomic increment with TTL in a single Lua script ensures the counter is consistent across all gateway.
- **X-RateLimit response headers are a UX contract** — `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Reset`, and `Retry-After` let well-behaved clients back off.
- **Warm-up exemption for new deployments** — cold instances behind a gateway should receive lower traffic for 30–60 seconds.
- **Per-tier limits require composable limiters** — a single Redis key can't express "100/sec global AND 10/sec per user AND 5/sec per expensive endpoint".

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A rate limiter for an API gateway handling 10 million requests per day is roughly 115 requests per second average with peaks at 3–5× — about 500–600 req/sec. The design must handle this throughput with sub-millisecond overhead per request, state shared across all gateway instances, and graceful degradation that doesn't cascade failures into the API itself.

**Choosing the algorithm:**
- Token bucket is my default: the bucket refills at a fixed rate (the allowed limit) but can hold burst capacity above the sustained rate; a user with a 100 req/sec limit can burst to 200 for a short spike without being rejected, which is the realistic behavior for well-behaved API clients
- Sliding window log is more precise for strict per-second enforcement: it counts requests in any trailing 60-second window, preventing the boundary exploit where 100 requests at 00:59 and 100 at 01:01 double the effective rate
- Fixed window is the simplest but allows that boundary exploit; use only for coarse-grained tiers where the doubling risk is acceptable

**Distributed state with Redis:**
- A single gateway instance can hold limits in memory, but a fleet of 10 gateway servers needs shared state; Redis atomic INCR + EXPIRE in a Lua script ensures the counter is consistent across all instances without race conditions
- The Lua script checks the current count, increments if below limit, and sets TTL atomically — this is the same approach Stripe and GitHub use in production
- For 10 million req/day with multiple dimensions (per user, per endpoint, per API key), you need composable independent limiters — one Redis key can't express all constraints simultaneously

**Response contract and graceful degradation:**
- Always return `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, and `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers so clients can back off intelligently before hitting 429
- When Redis is unavailable, fail open (allow traffic) rather than fail closed (block everything) — a temporary loss of rate limiting is less harmful than a complete API outage

I recommend token bucket with Redis-backed distributed state, Lua script atomics, and a fallback to in-memory per-instance limits when Redis is unavailable — protecting the API against Redis failure while maintaining reasonable fairness.

questions.question: Design a URL shortener service like bit.ly.
questions.title: Design a URL Shortener (bit.ly)
questions.direct_answer: Generate a unique short code per URL using base62 encoding of a distributed ID (Snowflake). Store the mapping in a database with a cache layer for hot URLs. The redirect service resolves short codes to long URLs with sub-10ms p99.

interviewer_intent.testing: Distributed ID generation, caching strategy, redirect performance, and analytics considerations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a random short code without collision detection — use sequential IDs for guaranteed uniqueness
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Snowflake ID encoding to base62, cache-aside pattern for hot URLs, and geographic distribution with CDN

sections.title: The Scale Math That Drives Every Design Decision
sections.content:
A URL shortener seems simple — map a short code to a long URL and redirect. But the scale numbers reveal the real engineering challenges. Bit.ly processes **billions of redirects per month**. At 1 billion redirects/month: **~400 reads/second average**, peaking at **2,000–4,000 reads/second**. If 10 million new URLs are shortened per month, that's **~4 writes/second** — reads dominate by 100:1.

This 100:1 read-to-write ratio drives the entire architecture: the read path must be **sub-10ms** (users click short links in browsers — slow redirects feel broken), which means aggressive caching. The write path can tolerate higher latency since shortening is an explicit API action.

The three core engineering problems: **generating globally unique short codes** without collisions or coordination, **serving redirects** at scale with low latency, and **handling analytics** (click counts, referrers, geography) without slowing down the redirect path. These three problems — unique ID generation, low-latency redirects, and non-blocking analytics — form the architectural backbone of every URL shortener at scale.

sections.title: Short Code Generation: Why Random Strings Are Dangerous
Read Path: Cache-Aside with Redis for Sub-10ms Redirects
Storage, Partitioning, and Geographic Distribution
sections.content:
**Storage estimation:** each URL mapping is approximately 500 bytes (short code + long URL up to 2048 chars + metadata). At 10M new URLs/month × 12 months × 5 years = **600M records × 500 bytes = 300 GB**. This fits comfortably on a single database server, so sharding is unnecessary for storage — but may be needed for read throughput at extreme scale.

The database schema is minimal: `short_code` (primary key, indexed), `long_url`, `created_at`, `user_id`, `expires_at`. Using the short code as the primary key means redirect lookups are primary key reads — the fastest possible database operation.

**Geographic distribution** matters when users are global. A click from Mumbai to a server in Virginia adds 150ms of network latency. Two strategies: **deploy read replicas in multiple regions** with the cache tier (Redis) in each region, so redirects are served locally. Or use a **global CDN with edge caching** — CloudFront can cache redirect responses at edge locations, serving 302s from the nearest POP.

For **custom short domains** (brands wanting `brand.co/xyz`), the system maps domain → tenant and resolves the short code within that tenant's namespace. This is a multi-tenant extension that requires the domain in the cache key: `url:{domain}:{shortCode}`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Base62 encoding of an auto-increment ID** — 6 characters of base62 gives 56 billion unique codes.
- **100:1 read-to-write ratio demands aggressive caching** — cache the short-code → URL mapping in Redis with a 24-hour TTL.
- **301 (permanent) vs 302 (temporary) redirect** — 301 tells browsers to cache the redirect permanently, reducing future load.
- **Cassandra or DynamoDB for the URL store** — single-key lookups by short code; no relational requirements; high read throughput.
- **Custom alias support requires collision detection** — user-provided aliases must check for existence before insertion.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A URL shortener maps short codes to long URLs and redirects users. The scale math shows the real challenge: the system needs to handle 10–100× more reads than writes because every shared link can be clicked millions of times. The architecture must optimize for the redirect hot path.

**Code generation strategy:**
- Base62 encoding of an auto-incrementing database ID is the cleanest approach: characters 0–9, a–z, A–Z give 62 characters; 6 characters gives 56 billion unique codes — more than enough for any realistic service
- Auto-increment IDs are predictable (a feature, not a bug — no collision risk, no retry logic); the database primary key becomes the short code after encoding
- Custom aliases require existence checks before insertion; use `INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS` to avoid race conditions on popular custom names

**The read-optimized architecture:**
- With a 100:1 read-to-write ratio, 90%+ of redirect traffic can be served without touching the database; cache the short-code → URL mapping in Redis with a 24-hour TTL
- The CDN layer handles the hottest links: a viral URL clicked 10 million times in an hour hits the CDN edge, which caches the 301 redirect response; origin sees only first-time requests from each CDN PoP
- Cassandra or DynamoDB for the URL store: single-key lookups by short code, high read throughput, no relational requirements — wide-column stores are ideal here

**The 301 vs 302 redirect decision:**
- 301 (Moved Permanently) tells browsers to cache the redirect locally — future clicks go directly to the destination without hitting your service at all; dramatically reduces load but eliminates your ability to count clicks
- 302 (Found/Temporary) forces every redirect through your service — enables click analytics, A/B testing, and link expiration at the cost of one server round-trip per click

I recommend 302 redirects with Redis caching for any service that needs analytics, and 301 only for static marketing links where click tracking has no value and maximum CDN efficiency matters.

questions.question: Design a notification service that sends email, SMS, and push notifications.
questions.title: Design a Notification Service (Email, SMS, Push)
questions.direct_answer: Decouple notification sending from business logic using a message queue. A notification service consumes events, determines channels, calls provider APIs (SendGrid, Twilio, FCM), and handles retries. Use per-channel queues for independent scaling and DLQ for failures.

interviewer_intent.testing: Event-driven architecture, multi-channel routing, retry/failure handling, and provider abstraction
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling SendGrid/Twilio directly from the order service — couples business logic to notification delivery
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention template management, user preferences (opt-out), deduplication for idempotency, and rate limiting per provider

sections.title: Why Notifications Can't Be a Direct API Call
sections.content:
When an order is placed, the order service needs to send a confirmation email, an SMS, and a push notification. The naive approach — calling SendGrid, Twilio, and Firebase directly from the order service — creates three problems: the order service is now **coupled** to three external vendors, any vendor outage **blocks** order completion, and adding a new channel (WhatsApp, in-app) requires **modifying the order service**.

A notification service decouples the business event from the delivery mechanism. The order service publishes an **event** ("order.placed"), and the notification service handles channel routing, template rendering, user preference checks, retry logic, and vendor API calls. The order service doesn't know or care how the user is notified.

The architecture is inherently **event-driven and asynchronous**. Notifications are not request-response — the user doesn't wait for the email to arrive before seeing their order confirmation. This means a message queue (Kafka or RabbitMQ) sits between the event producer and the notification service, providing durability, retry capability, and traffic buffering.

sections.title: The Four Components: Router, Renderer, Dispatcher, Tracker
sections.content:
The notification service is composed of four distinct responsibilities, each handling one concern independently.

The **Router** consumes events from the message queue and determines which channels to use for each notification. It checks user preferences (email opt-out, push enabled), applies business rules (critical alerts always send SMS regardless of preferences), and filters duplicates. A deduplication key — typically `{event_type}:{entity_id}:{timestamp_window}` — prevents the same notification from being sent twice when an event is retried.

The **Template Renderer** fills notification templates with event-specific data. Templates are stored separately (database or file system) and versioned, so marketing can update email copy without deploying code. The renderer handles localization — selecting the correct template for the user's language. Template rendering must be **fast and stateless** — no database queries beyond fetching the template itself.

The **Dispatcher** makes the actual vendor API calls — SendGrid for email, Twilio for SMS, Firebase for push. Each channel has its own dispatcher with independent retry logic and circuit breakers. If SendGrid is down, SMS and push continue unaffected. Dispatchers run in separate thread pools (bulkhead pattern) so a slow vendor can't block other channels.

The **Tracker** records delivery status — sent, delivered, bounced, opened, clicked. Vendor webhooks feed status updates back into the tracker. This data powers delivery dashboards and identifies systematic problems (high bounce rate on a specific email template, push notification delivery degradation on Android).

sections.title: Retry Strategy and Dead Letter Handling
Priority Queues and Rate Limiting at the Dispatch Layer
sections.content:
Not all notifications are equal. A password reset email must arrive in seconds. A weekly digest can wait hours. **Priority queues** separate critical notifications (OTP, security alerts, payment confirmations) from bulk notifications (marketing, digests, recommendations).

With RabbitMQ, this means separate queues with different consumer counts — the critical queue has more consumers and is processed first. With Kafka, use separate topics or partitions with dedicated consumer groups. The key principle: a burst of marketing emails should never delay a password reset.

**Vendor rate limiting** is the constraint most teams discover in production. SendGrid allows 100 emails/second on standard plans. Twilio charges premium rates above certain SMS volumes. The dispatch layer must **buffer and throttle** outbound calls to stay within vendor limits. This is a separate rate limiter from the API gateway limiter — it protects the vendor relationship, not the infrastructure.

The practical architecture at scale: critical notifications dispatch immediately through a high-priority path. Bulk notifications enter a **scheduled dispatch queue** that processes at a controlled rate, respecting vendor limits and user time zones (don't send marketing emails at 3 AM). This separation keeps critical notifications under 5 seconds end-to-end while bulk notifications accept minutes to hours of delay.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Queue per channel prevents slow SMS from blocking email** — a single queue means one overloaded provider delays all notifications.
- **Exponential backoff + dead-letter queue for provider failures** — provider outages are temporary; retry with doubling delay (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s).
- **Idempotency key per notification prevents duplicate sends** — at-least-once delivery means retries happen.
- **Template rendering at publish time locks in the snapshot** — render "Your order #123 ships tomorrow" when the event fires.
- **User preference service is a hard dependency** — check opt-out and contact info before routing to any channel.
- **Provider failover routes to backup on primary failure** — if Twilio returns 5xx, route to MessageBird within one retry.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A notification service that sends email, SMS, and push notifications must decouple event production from message delivery. The core design principle is that the order service, payment service, and every other business service should publish a business event ("order confirmed") and never know or care which channels deliver it or how.

**The event-driven architecture:**
- Business services publish events to a Kafka topic; the notification service subscribes and routes to the appropriate channel based on user preferences and event type; adding a new notification channel requires zero changes to any business service
- A separate preference service stores user contact info, opt-in/opt-out status, and preferred channels per event type; this is checked before routing to any channel — sending unsubscribed push notifications causes app uninstalls and regulatory risk

**Channel isolation prevents cascading delays:**
- A single shared queue means one SMS provider outage delays all email delivery; dedicate separate queues per channel — email queue, SMS queue, push queue — so each scales and fails independently
- Each channel has a dedicated consumer group with concurrency tuned to provider rate limits; Mailgun accepts 1,000 emails/sec; Twilio's SMS API is capped differently; configure per-channel

**Reliability patterns:**

sections.title: Why LIKE 'query%' Breaks at 100K Products
sections.content:
Autocomplete must respond in under **100ms** — users expect suggestions to appear as they type, and anything slower feels laggy. With a 10-million-product catalog, a naive SQL query (`SELECT name FROM products WHERE name LIKE 'lap%' ORDER BY popularity LIMIT 10`) scans a B-tree index for prefix matches. This works fine at 10,000 products. At 10 million, with concurrent users typing, the database buckles — each keystroke generates a query, and at 1,000 concurrent users typing at 3 characters/second, that's **3,000 queries/second** of full prefix scans.

The solution is a **purpose-built search index** — Elasticsearch with edge n-gram tokenization, or a Trie-based in-memory data structure. Both are optimized for prefix lookups: Elasticsearch pre-indexes every prefix at write time so reads are O(1) index lookups, while a Trie traverses the prefix path in O(k) where k is the query length.

The harder problem isn't just finding matches — it's **ranking** them. "lap" should return "laptop" before "lapel pin" because laptops are searched more frequently. Ranking combines prefix matching with popularity signals, recency, and personalization.

sections.title: Edge N-gram Indexing: How Elasticsearch Makes Prefix Search Fast
Ranking: Why the Most Popular Result Must Come First
sections.content:
Returning all products matching "lap" alphabetically is useless. The user almost certainly wants "laptop" — the most popular match. Ranking combines multiple signals, weighted by importance.

**Popularity score** (search frequency, purchase count) is the primary signal. Store a popularity counter per product, updated daily from analytics. Elasticsearch's `function_score` query multiplies the text match score by the popularity weight.

**Recency** matters for trending products. A product launched this week with moderate search volume should rank above a discontinued product with historical popularity. Apply a decay function that reduces the score of older products.

**Personalization** is the advanced tier. If the user previously browsed electronics, boost electronic products in autocomplete results. This requires a user profile service and adds latency — only worthwhile at scale.

The practical implementation scores results as `text_match * log(popularity + 1) * recency_decay`. The `log` prevents extremely popular products from completely dominating — a product with 10x the popularity should rank higher, but not 10x higher. Recency decay uses a half-life of 30 days: products older than 30 days get half the recency boost.

Caching adds another layer — the top 1,000 most common queries are cached in Redis with a 5-minute TTL. Since autocomplete queries follow a power-law distribution (a few prefixes account for most traffic), this cache serves 60–80% of requests without hitting Elasticsearch.

sections.title: Client-Side Optimization: Debounce, Minimum Length, and Cancellation
sections.content:
The autocomplete experience is as much about **what you don't send** as what you do. Three client-side optimizations reduce server load by 70–80%.

**Debouncing** delays the API call until the user pauses typing — typically 200–300ms. Without debounce, typing "laptop" fires 6 requests ("l", "la", "lap", "lapt", "lapto", "laptop"). With 300ms debounce, it fires 1 request ("laptop"). This single optimization eliminates the majority of autocomplete traffic.

**Minimum query length** of 2–3 characters prevents uselessly broad queries. A search for "l" matches millions of products — the results are meaningless and the query is expensive. Only send requests after 2+ characters.

**Request cancellation** aborts in-flight requests when the user types another character. If the user types "la" and then "p" before the "la" response arrives, cancel the "la" request — the results are already stale. In JavaScript, this uses `AbortController`; in mobile, cancel the Retrofit/URLSession request.

The combination of these three — debounce 300ms + min length 2 + cancellation — reduces autocomplete API calls by roughly 80% compared to sending a request on every keystroke. This is often the difference between needing 5 Elasticsearch nodes and needing 1.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Trie structure gives O(L) lookup where L = query length** — each node in the trie represents one character.
- **Pre-compute top-N suggestions per prefix** — at query time you want to read the answer, not compute it.
- **Prefix cache in Redis with serialized suggestion lists** — key is the lowercase prefix, value is a serialized list of {suggestion, score}.
- **Client-side debounce (150–200ms) reduces QPS by 3–5×** — users type faster than 100ms/character.
- **Personalization layer adds recency bias** — blend global popularity score with user's own query history using weighted sum.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Autocomplete must respond in under 100 milliseconds — users expect suggestions to appear as they type, and any perceived lag causes users to stop using it. The system at 10 million users generates roughly 50K–100K prefix queries per second at peak typing speed. This latency and throughput requirement drives every design decision.

**The trie data structure and precomputation:**
- A trie gives O(L) lookup time where L is the query length — O(1) per character regardless of total dictionary size; each node represents one character and points to children
- But traversing the trie at query time to find and rank all matches is too slow at this scale; instead, pre-compute the top-N suggestions for each prefix offline
- The analytics pipeline counts query frequencies hourly; the top 5 suggestions per prefix are written to Redis with the prefix as the key and a serialized ranked list as the value; query time is a single Redis GET

**Serving the suggestions:**
- A single Redis GET per prefix lookup takes ~1ms round-trip; for a 5-character query, you serve 5 Redis lookups (one per prefix length) in parallel or just the current prefix
- Client-side debounce (150–200ms) is the highest-leverage optimization: users type faster than 100ms per character, so debouncing reduces backend QPS by 3–5× without any perceptible latency increase
- CDN edge caching for common prefixes: "ja", "py", "co" — the top 1,000 most common prefixes handle 80% of queries; cache at the CDN edge for zero-latency serving

**Personalization and freshness:**
- Blend global popularity score with user's own recent query history using a weighted sum; prevents irrelevant suggestions for users with different vocabularies; fall back to global for new users
- Refresh the Redis precomputed suggestions every 15 minutes from the analytics pipeline; trending topics appear in autocomplete within 15 minutes of spiking

I recommend precomputed Redis serving with client-side debouncing as the core architecture, CDN caching for top common prefixes, and an offline analytics pipeline refreshing suggestions every 15 minutes.

sections.title: Why Relational Databases Can't Do Real-Time Rankings at Scale
sections.content:
A leaderboard needs to answer one question fast: **what rank is this user?** With a relational database, that's `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM scores WHERE score > ?` — a full table scan or index scan across millions of rows. At 10 million users with thousands of score updates per second, this query becomes the bottleneck. Every score update potentially changes the rank of every other user.

The traditional SQL approach — `ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 100` — works for displaying the top 100. But answering "what is user X's rank among 10 million users?" requires counting all users with higher scores, which is O(N). For a gaming platform processing 10,000 score updates per second, this is computationally prohibitive.

**Redis Sorted Sets** solve this with a data structure purpose-built for ranked data. Internally a skip list + hash table, sorted sets provide **O(log N) rank lookups and score updates** — for 10 million members, that's ~23 operations per lookup instead of 10 million. The rank of any member is computed in under 1ms.

sections.title: Redis Sorted Sets: The Data Structure Behind Every Leaderboard
Scaling Beyond One Sorted Set: Partitioned and Time-Windowed Leaderboards
sections.content:
A single Redis sorted set holds up to **~2^32 members** and works well for 10 million users. But production leaderboards need multiple dimensions: global, per-region, per-friend-group, daily, weekly, and all-time.

**Time-windowed leaderboards** use separate keys per period: `leaderboard:daily:2026-04-13`, `leaderboard:weekly:2026-W16`. Score updates write to all applicable keys simultaneously. At the end of each period, archive the key and create a new one. Daily leaderboards auto-expire with Redis TTL — set `EXPIRE leaderboard:daily:2026-04-12 172800` (48 hours) to keep yesterday's results accessible briefly.

**Per-group leaderboards** (friends, region, guild) use separate sorted sets per group. A user's score update fans out to their group keys. For friend-group leaderboards, the fan-out is bounded by the number of friends (~150 Dunbar's number). For regional leaderboards, partition by region ID.

The **memory math**: a sorted set with 10M members, each member ID ~20 bytes + 8 bytes score + skip list overhead ≈ **~500 MB**. Ten dimensional leaderboards = ~5 GB. Well within a single Redis instance's capacity (modern instances support 64+ GB), but monitor memory with `INFO memory` and set `maxmemory-policy` to reject writes rather than evict leaderboard data.

For rankings beyond Redis capacity (billions of users), **partitioned leaderboards with merge** work: shard users across multiple sorted sets by hash, query each shard for top-K, merge results. This is the approach mobile games with hundreds of millions of players use.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Redis Sorted Set with ZADD/ZREVRANK** — O(log N) writes and O(log N) rank lookups.
- **Write-through from game server to Redis** — game server updates score immediately on Redis; the database gets an async write via Kafka.
- **Batch database sync every 60 seconds** — writing to PostgreSQL on every score event creates unnecessary write amplification.
- **Sparse top-100 + user's neighborhood** — most users care about global top-100 and their rank ±10.
- **Pagination via ZREVRANGE with offset/count** — O(log N + M) where M is page size; Redis handles millions of ranked entries efficiently.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A real-time leaderboard for 10 million players requires ranking updates to appear within seconds of score changes. Relational databases with `ORDER BY score DESC` can't handle this — at this scale, a ranking query requires a full table scan or index scan over millions of rows on every update.

**The Redis Sorted Set as the core data structure:**
- Redis Sorted Set (ZSET) is the right answer: ZADD updates or inserts a score in O(log N); ZREVRANK returns a player's rank in O(log N); ZREVRANGE returns the top-N players in O(log N + N)
- Atomic operations prevent race conditions when two players earn the same score simultaneously; Redis single-threaded command processing ensures consistency without application-level locking
- For 10 million players, the sorted set occupies roughly 800MB–1.2GB of Redis memory — within a single instance's capacity

**The write path:**
- The game server writes the score directly to Redis (write-through) on every score event; this keeps the leaderboard always fresh
- The database gets an asynchronous write via Kafka every 60 seconds per player; batch updates reduce database write load by 60× without affecting the real-time leaderboard that users see

**What to show each user:**
- The global top-100 list is common to all users — serve it from a cached Redis ZREVRANGE call refreshed every 5 seconds
- Each user's own rank and neighborhood (±10 positions): two Redis calls — ZREVRANK for rank, ZREVRANGE with offset for neighbors; combine in a single pipeline call for sub-millisecond response
- Avoid returning more than 1,000 entries per request; pagination with ZREVRANGE(offset, count) is O(log N + M) where M is page size

I recommend Redis Sorted Set as the primary real-time store, async database sync for durability, and the sparse top-100 plus user neighborhood pattern to minimize the data returned per API call.

sections.title: The Problem: Why Payment APIs Must Handle Duplicate Requests
sections.content:
A user clicks "Pay" and the request times out. Did the payment go through? The client retries. If the server processes the payment again, the customer is charged twice. This isn't a theoretical edge case — it happens in production whenever networks are unreliable, which is always.

**Idempotency** means that making the same request multiple times has the same effect as making it once. For a payment API, this guarantees that retrying a failed request never creates a duplicate charge. Stripe, PayPal, and every serious payment processor implement this as a core API contract.

The mechanism: the client generates a unique **idempotency key** (a UUID) and sends it with the request. The server checks if it has already processed a request with that key. If yes, it returns the **original response** without processing again. If no, it processes the request and stores the result keyed by the idempotency key. The critical subtlety is what happens when two requests with the same key arrive **simultaneously** — this is where distributed locking enters the design.

sections.title: The Idempotency Key: What It Is and What It Cannot Be
The Concurrent Request Problem: Distributed Locking
End-to-End Payment Flow: Outbox Pattern for Consistency
sections.content:
Payment processing involves two operations that must be consistent: **charging the customer** (via payment gateway) and **recording the payment** (in the database). If the charge succeeds but the database write fails (server crash, network issue), the customer is charged with no record of the payment.

The **transactional outbox pattern** solves this. Instead of calling the payment gateway directly, write a payment event to an outbox table in the **same database transaction** as the order record. A separate processor reads the outbox and calls the payment gateway. If the gateway call fails, the outbox entry remains and is retried.

The flow: client sends payment with idempotency key, server acquires lock, writes order plus payment event to database in one transaction, releases lock, returns "payment pending." Outbox processor picks up the event, calls Stripe, and on success updates order status to "paid" and marks the outbox entry as processed.

This guarantees that if the order is recorded, the payment will eventually be processed. If the server crashes after the database write, the outbox processor retries. If it crashes before, neither the order nor the payment exists — clean state.

The trade-off is that payment is now **asynchronous**. The API returns "pending" immediately, and the client polls for the final status or receives a webhook. Stripe operates the same way — `PaymentIntent` starts as "processing" and transitions to "succeeded" asynchronously.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Idempotency key (UUID) per payment request** — client generates UUID on first attempt and reuses on retries.
- **Idempotency store: Redis with 24-hour TTL** — check for existing result before processing; if found, return the cached response immediately.
- **Exactly-once delivery requires database-level constraint** — Redis deduplication is best-effort.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A payment API must handle the fundamental problem of network unreliability. A user clicks "Pay," the request times out — did the charge happen? The client retries, and if the payment processor charges again, you've lost the customer. The solution is idempotency: every payment request carries a unique key, and the server guarantees that retrying with the same key produces the same outcome without double-charging.

**The idempotency key mechanism:**
- The client generates a UUID before the first attempt and sends it as a request header; on every retry of the same payment, the same UUID is reused
- The server uses the UUID as a unique key in a deduplication store; before processing, check if the key exists; if it does, return the cached response immediately without touching the payment processor
- The deduplication check and the payment processing must be atomic — use a database unique constraint on the idempotency key so concurrent retries can't both slip through and both charge

**Storage and TTL:**
- Redis for fast deduplication lookup with 24-hour TTL — covers any realistic retry window; the key maps to the cached response (success or failure) so retries get the exact same response body
- A database-level unique index provides the durable guarantee — if Redis fails, the unique constraint still prevents double-charges; both layers together give defense in depth

**Handling long-running payments:**
- 3D Secure authentication and some payment processors take 5–30 seconds; holding the HTTP connection open is not viable
- Return HTTP 202 Accepted immediately with a status endpoint URL; the client polls the status endpoint until COMPLETED or FAILED; this avoids client timeouts that trigger unnecessary retries

I recommend idempotency keys generated client-side with UUID, Redis deduplication with 24-hour TTL backed by a database unique constraint, and the 202 Accepted pattern for any payment flow that takes more than 2 seconds to complete.

sections.title: Why HTTP Polling Is a Non-Starter at Messaging Scale
sections.content:
A WhatsApp-scale system handles **2 billion registered users**, roughly **100 million daily active**, each sending ~40 messages per day. That is **4 billion messages daily ÷ 86,400 seconds ≈ 46,000 messages/second** average, with peaks at 3–5× during evening hours — **~200K msg/sec**. The real bottleneck is not message throughput but **connection count**: 100 million concurrent WebSocket connections across a fleet of gateway servers.

The most common design mistake is using **HTTP polling** — clients repeatedly ask "any new messages?" every few seconds. With 100M users polling every 5 seconds, that is **20 million requests/second**, of which 95% return nothing. This wastes server capacity and adds 2–5 seconds of artificial latency to every message. Persistent **WebSocket connections** solve both problems: the server pushes messages the instant they arrive, delivering sub-300ms latency.

Storage requirements compound the challenge: 4B messages/day × 500 bytes average = **2TB/day** of message data. With 1-year retention, that is **730TB** — ruling out any single-node relational database. Messages are write-heavy and read-sequentially (chat history scrollback), pointing to **Cassandra** or a similar LSM-tree store optimized for append-heavy workloads with partition-key locality.

sections.title: WebSocket Gateways and the Session Registry Pattern
sections.content:
Each client opens a **persistent WebSocket connection** to a gateway server. Modern gateway servers using epoll-based I/O can hold **500K–1M idle connections** on a single machine (32GB RAM, Linux kernel tuned with increased file descriptor limits). For 100M concurrent users, the system needs **100–200 gateway instances** behind a load balancer.

When a client connects, the gateway registers a session mapping in **Redis**: `session:{userId} → {gatewayId}`. When User A sends a message to User B, the message service looks up B's gateway in Redis — an O(1) operation — and forwards the message to that specific gateway, which pushes it down B's WebSocket. If User B has no Redis entry (offline), the message is persisted to the durable store and a **push notification** (FCM for Android, APNs for iOS) fires to wake the device.

The architecture keeps routing stateless even though connections are stateful.

```
Client A ──WebSocket──→ Gateway-3
                           │
                     ┌─────┴──────┐
                     │  Message   │
                     │  Service   │
                     └─────┬──────┘
                           │ lookup user B → Redis → gateway-7
                           │
                     Gateway-7 ──WebSocket──→ Client B
                           │
                     If offline → Cassandra + Push Notification
```

Gateway servers are **stateful** (they hold connections), but the message routing service is **stateless** — any instance can route any message by querying Redis. This separation matters for operations: you can roll gateway servers with connection draining while message services deploy independently and instantly.

sections.title: Cassandra for Message Storage: Partitioned by Conversation
sections.content:
Messages need a storage engine that excels at **high write throughput** and sequential reads (chat history scrollback). **Cassandra** fits naturally: its LSM-tree architecture is optimized for append-heavy workloads, and leaderless replication with tunable consistency gives multi-datacenter availability without complex shard management.

The schema places all messages for one conversation in a single partition, ordered chronologically by a time-ordered UUID.

```sql
CREATE TABLE messages (
    conversation_id  UUID,
    message_id       TIMEUUID,
    sender_id        UUID,
    content          TEXT,
    content_type     TEXT,
    media_url        TEXT,
    status           TEXT,
    created_at       TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);
```

Reading the last 50 messages is a single partition read with `LIMIT 50` — the most efficient query Cassandra can execute. Write consistency uses `LOCAL_QUORUM` (2 of 3 replicas in the local datacenter acknowledge) while reads use `LOCAL_ONE` for lower latency, since chat history tolerates brief staleness.

**Why not PostgreSQL?** At 46K writes/second average with 200K peaks, a single Postgres instance would need aggressive sharding from day one. Cassandra's built-in partitioning eliminates shard management overhead, and its leaderless design avoids single-writer bottlenecks. Each conversation's messages are co-located on the same partition, so scrollback reads never span multiple nodes.

sections.title: Message Ordering: Sequence Numbers Beat Vector Clocks
Group Messaging: When Fan-Out on Write Becomes Expensive
Failure Modes: What Breaks and How the System Self-Heals
sections.content:
**Gateway crash** — the user's WebSocket drops. The client reconnects (with exponential backoff and jitter) to any available gateway, re-registers in Redis, and pulls missed messages by sequence number. Messages queued during disconnection are durable in Cassandra, so nothing is lost.

**Redis (session registry) down** — gateways can't route messages to specific peers. The fallback is **topic-based broadcasting**: publish the message to a Kafka topic partitioned by user ID, and let each gateway consume messages for its connected users. Slower but functional. Redis Sentinel or Cluster provides HA to minimize this scenario's duration.

**Cassandra node failure** — replication factor 3 means losing one node has zero impact on reads or writes at `LOCAL_QUORUM`. Cassandra's hinted handoff and repair handle node recovery automatically with no operator intervention.

**Thundering herd on reconnection** — after a major outage, millions of clients reconnect simultaneously. Rate-limit reconnection with **jittered backoff** on the client side, and use connection admission control on gateways (reject with `Retry-After` header if at capacity). Without this, the reconnection storm can crash the gateways that just recovered.

**Message ordering violation** — network reordering can cause messages to arrive out of sequence. The per-conversation sequence number lets clients reorder locally. If a gap persists beyond 5 seconds, the client fetches missing messages from the REST API as a self-healing fallback.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **WebSocket + Redis session map for O(1) routing** — persistent connections deliver sub-300ms latency.
- **Cassandra partitioned by conversation_id** — LSM-tree architecture handles append-heavy message writes.
- **Server-assigned sequence numbers per conversation** — Redis INCR gives monotonically increasing IDs per conversation.
- **Fan-out on write for groups <100; fan-out on read for larger** — small groups copy message references to each member inbox (fast reads).
- **Offline message queue with 30-day retention** — Kafka topic per user for undelivered messages; consumer is the gateway.
- **End-to-end encryption: Signal Protocol** — X3DH key agreement on session establishment; Double Ratchet for forward secrecy.

A WhatsApp-scale chat system handles 100 million daily active users generating roughly 46,000 messages per second average, peaking at 200,000 during evening hours. The most important design decision is transport — HTTP polling disqualifies itself immediately because it requires 95% of requests to return empty responses and adds seconds of latency.

**The WebSocket gateway and routing:**
- Each client opens a persistent WebSocket connection to a gateway server; modern Linux servers with epoll-based I/O can hold 500K–1M idle connections with tuned file descriptor limits; 100M concurrent users needs 100–200 gateway instances
- When a client connects, the gateway registers a session mapping in Redis: `userId → gatewayId`; when User A sends to User B, the message service does an O(1) Redis lookup and forwards directly to B's gateway without broadcasting to all gateways
- Message delivery latency is consistently sub-300ms end-to-end with this architecture

**Storage — Cassandra for the message log:**
- Cassandra's LSM-tree architecture handles append-heavy write workloads; partition by conversation_id so all messages for one chat are co-located; cluster by TIMEUUID for chronological ordering
- 4 billion messages/day at ~1KB each = 4TB/day; with replication factor 3, that's 12TB/day of total storage; Cassandra scales horizontally by adding nodes, each absorbing 1/N of the new data

**The hard problems:**
- Message ordering: the server assigns a monotonically increasing sequence number per conversation using Redis INCR; clients detect gaps and request missing messages; simpler and sufficient compared to vector clocks
- Group fan-out: groups under 100 members use fan-out-on-write (pre-deliver to each member inbox); larger groups and broadcast channels use fan-out-on-read (store once, deliver on access) to avoid 10,000-write amplification per message
- Offline delivery: messages are retained in Cassandra; reconnecting clients replay from their last acknowledged sequence number

I recommend WebSocket gateways with Redis session routing, Cassandra for message storage, server-assigned sequence numbers for ordering, and the hybrid fan-out strategy with a configurable threshold between write and read fan-out.

sections.title: Scale Math: Why Naive Approaches Collapse
sections.content:
Twitter-scale numbers: **500 million tweets/day**, **300 million daily active users**, each following ~200 accounts on average. Each user opens their feed ~10 times/day → **3 billion feed reads/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 35,000 read QPS**, peaks at 100K+ QPS. Feed generation must complete in **< 200ms** including ranking.

The naive approach — "when User A opens their feed, query all 200 accounts they follow, fetch recent posts, merge and sort" — requires 200 database queries per feed load. At 35,000 QPS that is **7 million DB queries/sec** just for feed reads. This is the core problem: you must **pre-compute** feeds to avoid this read-time fan-out.

But pure pre-computation has its own problem. When a celebrity with 50 million followers posts, you'd need to write that post ID into 50 million users' feed caches. That single tweet triggers **50 million writes** — taking minutes to propagate. Twitter famously solved this with a **hybrid model**: pre-compute for regular users, compute on-the-fly for celebrities.

Storage: each feed entry is ~100 bytes (post ID + metadata). A user's feed cache holds 800 entries → 80KB per user. 300M users × 80KB = **24TB** of feed cache — fits in a Redis cluster.

sections.title: Hybrid Fan-Out Architecture
sections.content:
The system splits users into two categories based on follower count:

**Regular users (< 10K followers) — fan-out on write.** When they post, a fan-out service pushes the post ID into every follower's feed cache (a Redis sorted set keyed by `feed:{userId}`, scored by timestamp). With an average of 200 followers, this is 200 Redis writes per post — fast and manageable.

**Celebrity users (≥ 10K followers) — fan-out on read.** Their posts are NOT pushed into follower feeds. Instead, when a user loads their feed, the feed service fetches the pre-computed feed from Redis AND queries a small "celebrity posts" cache for any celebrities that user follows, then merges the two lists.

```
User posts a tweet:
    │
    ├── follower_count < 10K?
    │   YES → Fan-out on write:
    │         Kafka → Fan-out Workers → ZADD feed:{followerId} {timestamp} {postId}
    │         (for each follower)
    │
    └── follower_count ≥ 10K?
        YES → Store in celebrity_posts:{userId} only
              (merged at read time)

User reads their feed:
    │
    ├── ZREVRANGE feed:{userId} 0 49        (pre-computed feed)
    ├── For each celebrity the user follows:
    │   ZREVRANGE celebrity_posts:{celeb} 0 9  (recent posts)
    ├── Merge + rank + return top 50
```

The 10K threshold is tunable — Twitter reportedly used ~5K. The key insight: a small percentage of users (celebrities) create a disproportionate share of fan-out cost. Exempting them cuts total write amplification dramatically while adding only a few Redis reads per feed load.

sections.title: Data Model and Storage Layers
sections.content:
**Post storage (PostgreSQL or DynamoDB):**

```sql
CREATE TABLE posts (
    post_id       BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,   -- Snowflake ID
    user_id       BIGINT NOT NULL,
    content       TEXT,
    media_urls    JSONB,
    like_count    INT DEFAULT 0,
    retweet_count INT DEFAULT 0,
    reply_count   INT DEFAULT 0,
    created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    is_deleted    BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE
);

CREATE TABLE follows (
    follower_id   BIGINT,
    followee_id   BIGINT,
    created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_followee ON follows(followee_id); -- who follows me
```

**Feed cache (Redis sorted sets):**
- Key: `feed:{userId}` → sorted set of `(postId, timestamp)` — max 800 entries with `ZREMRANGEBYRANK` to cap
- Key: `celebrity_posts:{userId}` → recent 200 posts from celebrity accounts
- Key: `user_profile:{userId}` → cached user metadata for feed rendering

**Social graph (Redis or dedicated graph store):**
- `following:{userId}` → set of user IDs this user follows
- `followers:{userId}` → set of follower user IDs (used by fan-out workers)

The feed cache stores only **post IDs**, not full posts. The feed service hydrates IDs into full post objects by batch-fetching from a post cache (Redis) backed by PostgreSQL. This keeps feed entries tiny and avoids stale data — if a user edits their post, only the post cache needs updating, not millions of feed entries.

sections.title: Feed Ranking: Beyond Chronological Order
Consistency, Pagination, and Edge Cases
sections.content:
**Feed consistency on unfollow:** If User A unfollows User B, B's posts should disappear from A's feed. Two approaches: (1) lazily filter at read time — when rendering the feed, check if the author is still followed, or (2) eagerly remove B's posts from A's feed cache. Lazy filtering is simpler and handles most cases; eager removal is needed only if the unfollow is a block (safety requirement).

**Pagination with cursor-based scrolling:** Offset-based pagination breaks when new posts push items between pages. Use **cursor pagination** — the client sends the last-seen post ID or timestamp, and the server returns posts older than that cursor. Redis `ZREVRANGEBYSCORE` with the cursor score handles this naturally.

**Delete propagation:** When a user deletes a post, mark `is_deleted = true` in the post table. The feed cache contains only post IDs, so the hydration step naturally filters deleted posts. No need to remove the ID from millions of feed caches — eventual consistency through the hydration layer.

**New user cold start:** A new user with no follow graph has an empty feed. The feed service falls back to a **trending/recommended** feed generated by a batch job. As the user follows accounts and interacts, their personalized feed gradually replaces the default.

**Multi-region:** Deploy feed caches per-region (US-East, EU-West, APAC). The fan-out workers publish to Kafka, and regional consumers update regional Redis clusters. A user's feed reads always hit their nearest region. Cross-region follows work because the fan-out message propagates through Kafka replication.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Fan-out on write for <1,000 followers** — pre-compute feed at post time by writing to each follower's Redis feed list.
- **Celebrity problem: hybrid push-pull** — users with >10,000 followers skip pre-computation.
- **Feed Redis list: 1,000-post window per user** — store only the latest 1,000 post IDs per user in Redis.
- **Ranking model re-scores the feed** — raw chronological feed is replaced by an ML ranking score combining recency, engagement rate, and user affinity.
- **Dual database: Cassandra for writes, Elasticsearch for search** — Cassandra handles 500M writes/day.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A social media feed at Twitter scale handles 500 million posts per day and 3 billion feed renders per day. The fundamental design challenge is that writes (posts) are relatively rare but reads (feed loads) are orders of magnitude more frequent — the system must optimize aggressively for the read path while keeping writes manageable.

**Fan-out on write — the default for normal users:**
- When a user with 200 followers posts, write the post reference to each of those 200 followers' feed lists in Redis; feed reads become a single Redis list operation — O(1), regardless of who you follow
- Limit each Redis feed list to the latest 1,000 post IDs; older content is fetched from the timeline service on scroll; this bounds Redis memory to a manageable size
- This works for 99% of users who have fewer than 10,000 followers

**The celebrity problem — hybrid push-pull:**
- A user with 5 million followers would require 5 million write operations per post; fan-out-on-write is prohibitively expensive at this scale
- Celebrity accounts skip pre-computation; their posts are stored once and pulled at read time, merged with the pre-computed feed of the requesting user
- The threshold is configurable — typically 10,000–100,000 followers triggers the pull path

**Feed ranking:**
- Raw chronological feeds are replaced by a ranking model that scores each candidate post on recency, engagement rate, creator affinity, and content type preference
- The ranking score is computed offline by the ML pipeline and stored alongside the post ID in the feed list; retrieval fetches IDs, ranking scores are looked up in parallel
- Real-time signals (a post going viral in the last 5 minutes) are injected at read time by the trending service

I recommend fan-out-on-write for standard users with a celebrity threshold cutover to fan-out-on-read, Redis feed lists capped at 1,000 entries per user, and ML-based feed ranking as the baseline rather than chronological order.

sections.title: The Bandwidth Problem That Makes Chunking Non-Negotiable
sections.content:
Consider a service with **500 million users**, 100 million daily active, each storing ~2GB on average — **1 exabyte (1,000 PB)** total. Daily uploads: 50 million files with an average size of 500KB → **25TB ingested daily**, roughly **580 uploads/sec** average with peaks at 5–10× during business hours.

The most common design mistake is treating files as **monolithic blobs**. If a user edits a single paragraph in a 100MB document, the naive system re-uploads the entire 100MB. Multiply by millions of users making small edits throughout the day, and the bandwidth waste becomes staggering. Worse, deduplication becomes impossible — two users with the same file store it twice.

The foundational design principle is **separating metadata from file content**. Metadata (file names, paths, permissions, version history, chunk manifests) lives in PostgreSQL where ACID transactions ensure correctness for operations like rename, move, and share. File content is split into **chunks**, each content-hashed with SHA-256, and stored in S3. Identical chunks — across versions or across users — are stored exactly once. This separation lets each layer scale independently: PostgreSQL handles complex relational queries, S3 handles petabyte-scale blob storage with 11 nines of durability.

sections.title: Chunking and Deduplication: How One-Byte Edits Avoid Full Re-uploads
Metadata Service: ACID Where It Matters
sections.content:
File metadata requires **transactional consistency** that object storage cannot provide. Renaming a folder must atomically update all children's paths. Moving a file between folders must atomically update the parent reference. Sharing permissions must be checked on every access. PostgreSQL handles all of these naturally.

The schema models files and folders as a tree with parent references.

```sql
CREATE TABLE files (
    file_id        BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id        BIGINT NOT NULL,
    parent_id      BIGINT REFERENCES files(file_id),
    name           VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    is_folder      BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    latest_version INT DEFAULT 1,
    size_bytes     BIGINT,
    content_hash   VARCHAR(64),
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ,
    updated_at     TIMESTAMPTZ,
    is_deleted     BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    UNIQUE (user_id, parent_id, name)
);

CREATE TABLE file_versions (
    file_id      BIGINT REFERENCES files(file_id),
    version      INT,
    chunk_hashes JSONB,
    size_bytes   BIGINT,
    created_by   BIGINT,
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ,
    PRIMARY KEY (file_id, version)
);
```

Every save creates a new `file_versions` row with the updated chunk manifest. The `files` table always points to the latest version via `latest_version`. Old versions are retained for 30 days — users can restore previous versions within that window.

**Garbage collection** uses reference counting. Each chunk tracks how many file versions reference it via a `ref_count` column. When a version expires or is deleted, referenced chunks get their counts decremented. A background GC job periodically deletes chunks with `ref_count = 0` from S3, reclaiming storage without risking data loss for active versions.

Sharding strategy: partition by `user_id` so a single user's entire file tree lives on one shard. Cross-user sharing uses a `shared_access` table mapping `(file_id, grantee_user_id, permission_level)` that can reside on any shard since sharing lookups are infrequent compared to tree traversals.

sections.title: Sync Protocol: Change Logs and Conflict Resolution
sections.content:
The sync problem boils down to: "what changed since I last checked?" Dropbox solves this with a **change log** — a journal of every file mutation stamped with a globally monotonic sequence number.

Each client remembers the sequence number of the last change it processed. On sync, it requests `GET /changes?cursor=1001` and receives all mutations since then. For real-time responsiveness, combine **long-polling** (or WebSocket push) for immediate notification with periodic full sync as a consistency safety net.

```
Change Log:
seq=1001  user:42  MODIFY  /docs/report.pdf   v3
seq=1002  user:42  CREATE  /photos/beach.jpg   v1
seq=1003  user:42  DELETE  /tmp/draft.txt
seq=1004  user:42  MOVE    /docs/old.pdf → /archive/old.pdf
```

**Conflict resolution** arises when two devices edit the same file while both are offline. The Dropbox model handles this pragmatically:

1. Device A edits `report.pdf` (based on version 3) and syncs first → server accepts, creates version 4
2. Device B also edited `report.pdf` (based on version 3) and syncs later → server detects base version 3 ≠ current version 4
3. Server saves B's version as a **conflict copy**: `report (B's conflicted copy).pdf`
4. The user manually chooses which version to keep

This is deliberately simple. Google Docs uses **Operational Transform (OT)** for real-time collaborative editing within a single document, but for a file-level storage service where files include binary formats (images, videos, executables), automatic merging is impossible. Conflict copies are the correct general-purpose approach — predictable, auditable, and safe for any file type.

sections.title: Resumable Uploads, Security, and Performance Optimization
sections.content:
Large files spanning gigabytes cannot rely on a single HTTP connection surviving from start to finish. **Resumable uploads** let clients recover from interruptions without restarting. The client uploads chunks independently, each identified by its SHA-256 hash. If a connection drops mid-upload, the client asks the server which chunks it already received and uploads only the remaining ones. Google's resumable upload protocol uses this same chunk-level tracking approach.

**Security** layers protect data at every stage. Chunks are encrypted at rest in S3 using **AES-256 server-side encryption**. All transfers use TLS 1.3. For users requiring zero-knowledge storage, **client-side encryption** lets the user hold the key — the server stores only ciphertext. The trade-off: server-side search and preview generation become impossible with client-side encryption, since the server cannot read what it stores.

**Performance optimizations** improve the daily experience for active users. The client maintains a **local cache** of recently accessed chunks, reassembling files locally and downloading only missing chunks. For frequently shared files (company templates, team documents), serve chunks from a **CDN** to reduce origin load and improve download speed. Text-based files benefit from gzip compression before upload; already-compressed formats (JPEG, ZIP, MP4) should skip compression.

**Quota management** tracks each user's storage as `SUM(size_bytes)` across all active file versions. When two users share identical chunks, each user's quota still counts those chunks individually. The alternative — shared-chunk quota splitting — creates confusing billing when one user deletes their copy. Per-user counting is simpler and more predictable for customer support.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Chunked upload with resumable sessions** — split files into 4MB chunks; upload each with a session ID.
- **Content-addressable storage with SHA-256 deduplication** — hash each chunk before upload; if the hash exists in the store, skip upload entirely.
- **Delta sync sends only changed blocks** — compute block-level diffs on the client; send only modified 4MB blocks rather than the whole file.
- **S3 for blob storage, metadata in PostgreSQL** — files as objects in S3; file metadata (path, size, version, owner) in a relational database.
- **Conflict resolution: last-write-wins with version vectors** — track vector clocks per device; on conflict, keep both versions and present to user.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A file storage and sync service at Google Drive scale handles 500 million users storing roughly 2GB each on average — 1 exabyte of total storage. The design must handle large file uploads reliably, sync changes across multiple devices efficiently, and serve files with low latency globally.

**Upload architecture:**
- Split files into 4MB chunks before upload; each chunk uploads independently with a resumable session ID; on network failure, resume from the last successful chunk without re-uploading what the server received
- Content-addressable storage: compute SHA-256 of each chunk before upload; if the hash already exists in the store (another user uploaded the same file), skip the upload entirely; at Dropbox scale this eliminates 30–40% of upload bandwidth through cross-user deduplication
- S3 (or GCS) for blob storage; the database stores only metadata — file path, owner, chunk hashes, version history, sharing permissions

**Delta sync — efficient for large files:**
- Instead of uploading the entire file on every change, compute block-level diffs on the client; send only the modified 4MB blocks
- For a 2GB virtual machine image where 50MB changed, delta sync sends 50MB instead of 2GB — a 40× reduction
- The client maintains a local block hash map; the sync service sends the set of changed block hashes; the client uploads only those blocks

**Conflict resolution:**
- When two devices edit the same file simultaneously, a conflict occurs; most services implement last-write-wins as the default with conflict copies preserved
- Version vectors track which device wrote which version; on conflict, both versions are kept and presented to the user for resolution
- For collaborative documents (like Google Docs), Operational Transformation or CRDT-based algorithms enable real-time concurrent editing without conflicts

I recommend S3 for blob storage, content-addressable chunk deduplication, delta sync for frequently modified large files, and last-write-wins with conflict copy preservation as the default conflict resolution strategy.

sections.title: Bandwidth Dominates Everything: Why You Can't Serve the Original File
sections.content:
YouTube-scale: **500 hours of video uploaded every minute**, **1 billion hours watched per day**. The dominant cost is outbound bandwidth — at an average streaming bitrate of 5 Mbps, one billion watch-hours daily consumes approximately **5 exabytes of bandwidth per day**. CDN costs dwarf compute, storage, and every other operational expense.

The most common design mistake is **streaming the original uploaded file** directly. A user uploads a 4K video at 50 Mbps — streaming it to a viewer on a 3G mobile connection means constant buffering. Streaming it to a viewer with a 1080p screen wastes 75% of the bandwidth on resolution they can't display. The system must **transcode** every upload into a ladder of resolution-bitrate pairs (240p through 4K) and let the player select the appropriate quality dynamically.

The architecture separates into three independent subsystems with fundamentally different bottlenecks: the **upload and transcoding pipeline** (CPU-bound), the **metadata service** (IOPS-bound — titles, search, view counts, recommendations), and the **content delivery network** (bandwidth-bound — serving video segments globally). Each scales independently because adding CDN capacity doesn't solve a transcoding bottleneck.

sections.title: The Transcoding Pipeline: DAG-Based Parallel Processing
sections.content:
Raw video upload follows a **resumable protocol** — videos can be gigabytes, and mobile connections are unreliable. The client uploads directly to S3 via a pre-signed URL, bypassing the API server. On upload completion, an S3 event notification kicks off the transcoding pipeline.

Transcoding is not a single step — it is a **directed acyclic graph (DAG)** of independent tasks that run in parallel.

```
Raw Upload (S3)
    │
    ├─→ Audio extraction ─→ AAC encode ─→ ┐
    ├─→ 240p transcode ──────────────────→ │
    ├─→ 480p transcode ──────────────────→ ├─→ HLS/DASH packaging
    ├─→ 720p transcode ──────────────────→ │       │
    ├─→ 1080p transcode ─────────────────→ │       ├─→ Quality check
    ├─→ 4K transcode ────────────────────→ ┘       │
    ├─→ Thumbnail generation                       ├─→ CDN distribution
    └─→ Content moderation (ML)                    │
                                                   └─→ Mark as ready
```

All five resolution transcodes run on separate machines simultaneously. A 10-minute video might take 20 minutes to transcode serially but only 5 minutes with parallel workers. Workers are **containerized FFmpeg instances** on Kubernetes, auto-scaling based on queue depth.

Each resolution maps to a target bitrate for its intended device class.

| Resolution | Bitrate | Target Device |
|---|---|---|
| 240p | 400 Kbps | 2G/3G mobile |
| 480p | 1 Mbps | Standard mobile |
| 720p | 2.5 Mbps | Tablet/laptop |
| 1080p | 5 Mbps | Desktop |
| 4K | 16 Mbps | Smart TV |

Each resolution is encoded in at least two codecs: **H.264** for universal compatibility and **H.265 (HEVC) or VP9** for 30–50% bandwidth savings on supporting devices. A 10-minute video produces roughly 50 output files across all resolution-codec combinations.

sections.title: Adaptive Bitrate Streaming: Why Buffering Is a Solved Problem
sections.content:
Videos are not served as monolithic files. Each transcoded variant is segmented into **6-second chunks**, and a manifest file lists all available quality levels. The player downloads the manifest, measures available bandwidth, and requests segments at the appropriate quality.

**HLS (HTTP Live Streaming)** uses an `.m3u8` master playlist that advertises each quality level.

```
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=400000,RESOLUTION=426x240
/video/abc123/240p/playlist.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1000000,RESOLUTION=854x480
/video/abc123/480p/playlist.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=2500000,RESOLUTION=1280x720
/video/abc123/720p/playlist.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=5000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080
/video/abc123/1080p/playlist.m3u8
```

The player starts by estimating bandwidth, picks the highest quality the connection supports, and begins downloading segments. If bandwidth drops mid-video — the user walks into an elevator — the player **switches to a lower bitrate on the next segment** without rebuffering. If bandwidth improves, it switches back up. This is **adaptive bitrate streaming (ABR)**, and it is why modern video players rarely buffer.

The critical architectural insight: segments are **ordinary HTTP files** cached by standard CDN infrastructure. HLS and DASH won the protocol war precisely because they piggyback on existing HTTP and CDN investment. Every segment request is a standard GET, cacheable at every layer of the CDN hierarchy. No proprietary streaming server is required — just a web server or CDN serving static files.

Each quality level has its own segment playlist listing individual `.ts` (MPEG-TS) or fragmented MP4 chunks. The player walks through segments sequentially, requesting the next segment before the current one finishes playing to maintain a 2–3 segment playback buffer.

sections.title: CDN Cache Hierarchy: Keeping Origin Load Manageable
sections.content:
Without a CDN, serving 1 billion hours of video per day from origin servers would require petabits of bandwidth from a few data center locations. The CDN distributes content to **200+ edge PoPs** worldwide, placing segments physically close to viewers.

The cache hierarchy has three tiers, each absorbing a layer of traffic.

```
Viewer → Edge PoP (city-level, 200+ locations)
              │ cache miss
              → Regional cache (continental, ~10 locations)
                    │ cache miss
                    → Origin shield (single cache before S3)
                         │ cache miss
                         → S3 origin (2–3 locations)
```

**Cache hit rates** for video are excellent. A popular video's segments are requested millions of times, but the content is immutable once transcoded. Typical CDN hit rate for popular content: **95%+**. Long-tail content (older videos with few views) has lower hit rates, but the **origin shield** prevents thundering herd: all regional caches miss to a single origin shield, which absorbs duplicate requests and forwards only one to S3.

**Cost optimization levers** at the CDN layer drive significant savings. **Codec efficiency** is the largest lever — H.265/VP9 delivers equivalent perceptual quality at 30–50% less bitrate than H.264. At exabyte-scale daily delivery, this codec migration directly halves the CDN bill. **Per-title encoding** (Netflix's approach) analyzes each video's visual complexity and generates custom bitrate ladders — an animated movie needs far less bandwidth than an action film at equivalent perceived quality. **Predictive caching** preloads trending content to edge PoPs before peak hours, using recommendation engine signals to anticipate demand.

sections.title: View Counting at Scale and Content Moderation
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Transcoding pipeline: FFmpeg in distributed workers** — raw video → multiple resolutions (360p/720p/1080p/4K) and formats (H.264/H.265/VP9/AV1).
- **Adaptive bitrate streaming (HLS/DASH)** — segment video into 2–10 second chunks at each quality level.
- **CDN for video delivery, not origin** — 99% of video playback traffic hits CDN edge nodes; origin serves only uploads and the 1% of rare/cold content.
- **Metadata in Cassandra, search in Elasticsearch** — video metadata (title, description, tags, creator) written to Cassandra for high write throughput.
- **View count approximation with HyperLogLog** — exact view counting at YouTube scale requires distributed coordination.
- **Content moderation pipeline** — computer vision models run on every uploaded video asynchronously; flagged content goes to human review queue.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
YouTube ingests 500 hours of video per minute and serves 1 billion hours of video per day. The design splits into two very different problems: the ingest and transcoding pipeline (write-heavy, batch processing) and the streaming delivery path (read-heavy, latency-critical).

**Video ingest and transcoding pipeline:**
- Raw uploaded video goes directly to object storage (S3); a transcoding job is published to a Kafka queue; distributed FFmpeg workers consume jobs and produce multiple resolution variants (360p, 720p, 1080p, 4K) and formats (H.264 for compatibility, H.265 for storage efficiency, AV1 for lowest bitrate)
- 1 hour of 1080p H.264 video is roughly 8GB raw; H.265 transcoding reduces this to 4GB at equal quality — significant storage savings at YouTube scale
- A 1-hour video requires 5–10 minutes of transcoding time distributed across a worker cluster; auto-scaling the worker fleet based on Kafka consumer lag handles upload traffic spikes

**Adaptive bitrate streaming (ABR):**
- Video is segmented into 2–10 second chunks at each quality level; the manifest file (HLS .m3u8 or DASH .mpd) lists all available quality levels and chunk URLs
- The client player monitors current download bandwidth and selects the highest quality that can be downloaded faster than it's being played; seamless quality switches without buffering or interruption
- Segment durations are 2 seconds for live streaming (low latency) and 6–10 seconds for VOD (better CDN cache efficiency)

**CDN delivery at scale:**
- 99% of video playback traffic hits CDN edge nodes; origin serves only uploads and rare/cold content; CDN serves popular content from the nearest geographic node, reducing latency from 150ms to 5ms
- View count approximation: exact counting at YouTube scale requires distributed coordination across thousands of servers; HyperLogLog gives ±1% accuracy with 12KB memory per counter

I recommend a Kafka-driven transcoding pipeline, HLS/DASH adaptive bitrate with 6-second segments for VOD, CDN delivery for all video content, and HyperLogLog for view count aggregation.
